text._main: The lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) and the anterior rami of S1–S4 join on the front of piriformis. Almost every branch leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen: the superior gluteal nerve above piriformis, the rest below it. BLOCK

Pudendal nerve block

Injection beside the pudendal nerve at the ischial spine, between the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments, by a transgluteal (ultrasound) or transvaginal route. For perineal, anal and penile surgery, and second-stage labour. Spread to the sciatic nerve can briefly weaken the leg.

Target: Ultrasound: ischial spine with the pudendal artery and nerve medial to it, in the plane between the two ligaments, deep to gluteus maximus.

BLOCK

Deep cervical plexus block

Injection at the C2, C3 and C4 transverse processes (or one injection at C3–C4 deep to the prevertebral fascia), blocking the rami and both cutaneous and motor branches. Phrenic palsy is common (up to about 60%), so avoid it if a hemidiaphragm paralysis would not be tolerated and never block both sides. Other risks: vertebral artery, intrathecal or epidural injection.

Target: Transverse processes of C2–C4 on a line from the mastoid to Chassaignac’s tubercle (C6); ultrasound: deep to the prevertebral fascia at the C3 or C4 transverse process, away from the vertebral artery and foramen; aspirate and inject slowly.

BLOCK

Lumbar plexus block (psoas compartment)

Local anaesthetic goes into the posterior part of psoas major at L3–L4 or L4–L5, where the roots and divisions lie; used for hip and femoral surgery. A deep block with real risks: epidural or intrathecal spread, local anaesthetic toxicity, retroperitoneal haematoma (follow neuraxial anticoagulation rules) and renal puncture at higher levels.

Target: Ultrasound at L3–L4: transverse flank scan (shamrock view: psoas, quadratus lumborum, erector spinae around the transverse process) or paramedian sagittal scan (trident view), often with nerve stimulation (quadriceps twitch).

Infrainguinal fascia iliaca block

Local anaesthetic goes deep to fascia iliaca just below the inguinal ligament, at the junction of its lateral and middle thirds, and spreads under the fascia. Simple, safe analgesia for hip and femoral fractures; obturator spread is unreliable.

Target: Transverse probe below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral nerve and artery; needle tip under fascia iliaca on iliopsoas.

BLOCK

Femoral nerve block

Local anaesthetic around the femoral nerve at the inguinal crease, lateral to the artery and deep to fascia iliaca; for hip and femoral shaft fractures and knee or anterior thigh surgery (weak quadriceps: fall risk). The "3-in-1" spread to the LFCN and obturator is unreliable, especially to the obturator.

Target: Transverse probe at the inguinal crease: nerve lateral to the femoral artery, under fascia iliaca. Twitch: quadriceps ("patellar dance").

BLOCK

PENG block (pericapsular nerve group)

Local anaesthetic is laid on the bone between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, deep to the psoas tendon, to reach the articular branches of the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves. Aims for hip analgesia that spares the quadriceps, though large volumes can reach the femoral nerve.

Target: Transverse probe over the AIIS, then rotated about 45° to line up with the pubic ramus: AIIS, iliopubic eminence, psoas tendon, femoral artery medially.

BLOCK

Obturator nerve block (proximal, interfascial)

Local anaesthetic goes into the plane between pectineus and obturator externus, just below the obturator canal, to block the nerve before it divides. Used to stop the adductor jerk during bladder tumour resection, for adductor spasm, and to add to hip or knee analgesia.

Target: Transverse probe at the inguinal crease, medial to the femoral vein; aim for the fascial plane between pectineus and obturator externus.

Ilio-inguinal and iliohypogastric block

Local anaesthetic goes between internal oblique and transversus abdominis just medial and superior to the ASIS, where both nerves run in this plane. Used for inguinal hernia repair, orchidopexy and groin incisions; the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve is not blocked.

extra.sacral/parasacral:
Details

BLOCK

Parasacral sciatic block (Mansour)

Local anaesthetic is placed on the sacral plexus as it leaves the greater sciatic foramen, deep to piriformis, so it reaches the sciatic nerve and usually its proximal branches. For hip, thigh, knee and below-knee surgery with a lumbar plexus or femoral block. Too deep risks the pelvic vessels and viscera.

Target: Lateral position. 6 cm caudal to the posterior superior iliac spine on the line to the ischial tuberosity; ultrasound shows the plexus between the ilium and the ischium, deep to piriformis.

Anterior sciatic block

Supine approach from the front of the proximal thigh: the needle passes medial to the femur to the sciatic nerve deep (posterior) to adductor magnus. Useful when the patient cannot be turned.
